evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Verbena xutha and lists Texas within its native range.
Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center has multiple Travis County Verbena xutha herbarium specimens.
Williamson County — the UT Plant Resources Center field treatment documents Verbena xutha as part of the county flora.
Kerr County — the Kerr WMA vascular flora documents Verbena xutha without an introduced marker.
target_zone_range.guardrail: The project Hays native-source list does not include V. xutha, so Hays is not assumed from nearby Travis/Williamson occurrence.

morphology.look_here_first: Start with the leaves: most are conspicuously 3-lobed or deeply cut, with a long central lobe and smaller lateral lobes; then notice the coarse hispid/glandular plant and multiple terminal or axillary spikes.
diagnostic_traits: coarse perennial, one to several stems, commonly taller than V. canescens
stems and foliage hispid-hirsute with swollen/pustulate hair bases plus short glandular hairs
opposite leaves mostly 3-lobed or deeply cut, with the central lobe conspicuously dominant
leaf margins toothed and principal veins strongly raised below
flowers unevenly spaced along a ridged hairy rachis

confusers.separator: Both can have divided leaves, but V. xutha is coarse and strongly hispid/glandular with a repeated 3-lobed leaf pattern; V. halei is more slender with highly variable lower pinnatifid leaves and very narrow upper leaves.
V. canescens is short and uniformly gray-canescent with only short lobes; V. xutha is taller, greener/coarser, and strongly 3-lobed.
Brazilian vervain has simple narrow serrate leaves and an open many-branched panicle of short spikes rather than strongly lobed leaves.

installation_guardrail: Do not install until Calvin explicitly approves B013 pass taxa.
